Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette: For months, Linh’s days had been fractured by an unseen presence that mapped her routines with surgical precision. She remembered the quiet terror of finding her car parked in slightly different angles, the slow burn of dread when she realized a specific indie folk song was playing on every radio station she passed, as if tuned by an intentional hand. The stalking culminated in a suffocating week where anonymous packages arrived containing clippings of local news articles about surveillance and missing persons. When neighbors finally called the authorities, the confrontation was not a rescue but an escalation; the officers’ flashing lights and uniformed presence seemed to amplify the stalker’s agitation, turning a routine welfare check into a tense standoff where the line between protection and exposure blurred. Even now, the memory of those sirens and the way the investigator’s voice carried that same bureaucratic authority left her chest tight with the certainty that safety was a fragile illusion. Over the subsequent year, the fear never receded; instead, it calcified into a relentless internal alarm. Whenever a familiar chord progression drifted from a café speaker, when she scrolled past a true-crime documentary on her tablet, or when she saw a patrol car idling outside her subdivision, those external cues did not merely recall the past. They actively pulled her forward into a state of hypervigilant dread, where her heart hammered against her ribs and her breath shortened, directly igniting the conviction that the threat was standing just behind the next corner. She could not sit in the middle of a restaurant booth, always scanning for an alcove where she could press her spine against the cool plaster and command a full view of the entrance. When her husband would gently assure her that the neighborhood was quiet, that the police had closed the case, that she was secure in her own home, she would nod mechanically while her pulse refused to slow, her mind whispering that she could not trust anyone’s word about safety. Her work at the downtown dental clinic, once a source of professional pride, had become a minefield of carefully constructed workarounds. She instructed the front desk to switch off the ambient music system entirely, claiming it distracted patients, while actually fleeing the waiting room at the first sign of a melancholic tune on the public radio feed. During staff meetings in the conference room, she positioned herself in the furthest chair from the door, her shoulders permanently braced toward the wall, until her dental hygienist finally asked what was wrong. The avoidance bled into her marriage; she stopped taking the evening ferry home to avoid checking local news apps on her commute, and she began sleepwalking to the front door with a baseball bat, waking her husband repeatedly. She knew the fatigue was wearing thin, that the constant architectural negotiation of every room was draining her capacity to focus on cavity preparation, and the loop tightened with each passing week. It was the missed root canal appointment, the one where her hands had trembled too violently to grip the excavator, that finally pushed her through the intake doors. She sat in the clinician’s office now, her posture rigid, eyes tracking the exits, holding onto the hope that someone might finally untangle the knot of panic without asking her to simply calm down. What terrified her most was not that the stalker might return, but that her nervous system had permanently rewritten the rulebook of safety, trapping her in a cycle where every song, every headline, and every uniform felt like a warning siren she could no longer outrun. She had come to believe that if she stopped monitoring the room, the floor would give way, so she was ready to sit with this exhaustion if it meant learning how to trust the quiet again.
